newsitem.title: CHINA: China says bomb attacks in Moslem Xinjiang solved.
newsitem.headline: China says bomb attacks in Moslem Xinjiang solved.

text.p: China said on Wednesday it had arrested several suspects and solved last week's bomb attacks that killed nine people and wounded 74 in the restive far western region of Xinjiang.

Those in custody were suspected of having made and planted the bombs that went off on buses in the regional capital Urumqi or of having sold detonators for the explosives, the official Xinjiang Daily said.
"The February 25 public bus bomb attacks have been solved after police investigations and with the support and assistance of all ethnic groups," it said in a front-page report.
Police were interrogating the suspects and hunting for others still at large, the newspaper said.
It called the bombing attacks a "planned and coordinated act of destruction by a terrorist group".
Three bombs exploded within minutes in Urumqi on February 25 in an apparently coordinated attack that coincided with funeral rites in Beijing for paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.
A fourth bomb failed to explode.

Three people died on the spot, six died later in hospital and 74 people were wounded, an official told Reuters by telephone on Wednesday. A source has said most of the victims were students on their way home from school.
The newspaper appealed in an editorial for ethnic unity.
"We should resolutely not do or say whatever is detrimental to ethnic unity," it said. "We must be on alert against the small group of bad people engaging in terrorist activities.
"If they stick out their heads, we should resolutely defeat their plot in accordance with the law," it said. "We will not allow them to trample on the law and sabotage stability."
Moslem separatists want to set up an independent "East Turkestan" in Xinjiang, home to many Turkic-speaking people, including those of the Uighur ethnic minority.
Exiled Uighur nationalists in neighbouring Kazakhstan on Tuesday claimed responsibility for the bombings and for a similar, previously unreported, attack on Monday.
A Chinese government official in Xinjiang denied there had been a blast on Monday.
Hong Kong's Sing Tao Daily newspaper said on Wednesday that paramilitary and riot police had been sent to reinforce Xinjiang and another frequent flashpoint, the Himalayan region of Tibet.
The Lanzhou Military Region, which oversees Xinjiang, was on alert against further unrest in the oil-rich area, which borders Central Asia, the newspaper said.

Unrest along China's borders, one of Beijing's chief security fears, was highlighted by Premier Li Peng on Saturday in his annual government work report to the National People's Congress, the nation's parliament.
Li did not mention the Xinjiang blasts, which have also been ignored by the official media in Beijing, but vowed to take a tough line on separatism.

In February, an anti-Chinese riot by local Uighurs broke out in Yining in Xinjiang. Chinese officials said nine people were killed in the riot -- one of the largest and most violent demonstrations for independence in Xinjiang since the 1949 communist takeover.

China also faces sporadic outbursts of unrest in Tibet, which has been under tight security since 1959 when troops put down an anti-Chinese uprising and sent the region's spiritual leader, the Dalai Lama, fleeing into exile in India.
